prerequisites: RHEL/CentOS 7-era system libraries: libssl.so.10 + libcrypto.so.10 (RHEL's OpenSSL 1.0.2 soname), libicuuc.so.50/libicui18n.so.50, libunwind.so.8, libuuid, libcurl, libgssapi_krb5, zlib
recipes.min_os: RHEL/CentOS 7 (and binary-compatible distros) x64 only; glibc 2.14+
recipes.notes: The plan's .NET Core 1.1 Linux file is the RHEL-specific tarball (dotnet-rhel-x64.1.1.13.tar.gz); 1.x had no portable linux-x64 runtime. Its native libraries link RHEL 7 sonames directly (libssl.so.10, ICU 50), and 1.x has no globalization-invariant mode, so it will not run on current distros. Unpacked and the muxer ran here (Ubuntu 24.04), but no app could run, so this counts as untested. The 1.x muxer has no --list-runtimes; `dotnet --info` without an SDK prints 'Did you mean to run dotnet SDK commands?' and exits 145, which only proves the host starts. Verify properly by running the app's dll. How to launch a framework-dependent app from this private copy: run the MUXER with the app's dll, "{runtime_dir}/dotnet" "<app>/app.dll". The muxer looks for host/fxr and shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App only relative to its own location. Tested: it ignores DOTNET_ROOT, and two copies side by side each resolve their own framework. Do NOT rely on the app's generated apphost (app.exe / ./app): it looks at DOTNET_ROOT_<ARCH>, then DOTNET_ROOT(x86) on 64-bit Windows for 32-bit apps, then DOTNET_ROOT, then the global location (registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\dotnet\Setup\InstalledVersions\<arch>\InstallLocation or %ProgramFiles%\dotnet on Windows; /etc/dotnet/install_location, then /usr/share/dotnet or /usr/lib/dotnet on Linux; /usr/local/share/dotnet on macOS). Tested: without DOTNET_ROOT it failed with 'You must install .NET'; with DOTNET_ROOT set it used the private copy. If an apphost must be used, set DOTNET_ROOT and DOTNET_ROOT_<ARCH> to {runtime_dir} in the app's process environment only. Clear variables a user may have set globally that would reach into the private runtime: DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS, DOTNET_ADDITIONAL_DEPS, DOTNET_SHARED_STORE, DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD*, CORECLR_ENABLE_PROFILING/CORECLR_PROFILER*, and COMPlus_* / DOTNET_* runtime knobs. Only Microsoft.NETCore.App is in this archive: apps that need ASP.NET Core (Microsoft.AspNetCore.App) or WinForms/WPF (Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App) need those runtime archives unpacked into the same {runtime_dir} (they add shared/<name>/<ver>), and the plan does not include them. A patch roll-forward inside the folder works (tested: an app built for 8.0.0 ran on 8.0.31, and a netcoreapp2.1 app ran on 2.2.5 through the default Minor roll-forward). Running on a newer major needs rollForward Major/LatestMajor in the app's runtimeconfig.json (3.0+). Nothing is written outside {runtime_dir} at install time. At run time the runtime creates $TMPDIR/dotnet-diagnostic-<pid>-*-socket and clr-debug-pipe-<pid>-* (removed on a clean exit; DOTNET_EnableDiagnostics=0 turns them off). If the app opens a CurrentUser X509Store it writes ~/.dotnet/corefx/cryptography/x509stores. No NuGet or SDK caches are involved because this is a runtime, not an SDK (tested: a runtime-only run left the test HOME and TMPDIR empty). The unpacker must keep exec bits (dotnet, createdump). The archives have no leading directory, so strip_components is 0.

launch.notes: Start the app as `dotnet <app>.dll` through this private dotnet, which only uses its own folder. DOTNET_ROOT is for an app's own .exe launcher; DOTNET_MULTILEVEL_LOOKUP=0 stops Windows 1.x-6.0 preferring a newer global install. 2.2/3.1 on new Linux distros may need CLR_ICU_VERSION_OVERRIDE (see recipe notes).

recipes.notes: IMPORTANT for the base installer's unzip: the 2.2 zips (dotnet-runtime-2.2.5-win-x64/x86/arm.zip and 2.2.1-win-arm64.zip) store entry names with BACKSLASH separators (e.g. 'host\fxr\2.2.5\hostfxr.dll'), which breaks the zip spec. The unzipper must treat '\' as a directory separator, or it will create files literally named 'host\fxr\...' (on Linux) or fail to create parent folders. Multi-level lookup is ON by default in these hosts (2.2-6.0) on Windows: the host compares the frameworks in {runtime_dir} with those in the global %ProgramFiles%\dotnet (or %ProgramFiles(x86)%\dotnet for 32-bit) and picks the most appropriate version from the two, so a newer global patch of the same major wins over the private one. That breaks isolation and reproducibility. Always launch with DOTNET_MULTILEVEL_LOOKUP=0 in the app's environment (only in the app's environment, never machine-wide). Tested: without DOTNET_ROOT it failed with 'You must install .NET'; with DOTNET_ROOT set it used the private copy. If an apphost must be used, set DOTNET_ROOT and DOTNET_ROOT_<ARCH> to {runtime_dir} in the app's process environment only. Clear variables a user may have set globally that would reach into the private runtime: DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS, DOTNET_ADDITIONAL_DEPS, DOTNET_SHARED_STORE, DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD*, CORECLR_ENABLE_PROFILING/CORECLR_PROFILER*, and COMPlus_* / DOTNET_* runtime knobs. Only Microsoft.NETCore.App is in this archive: apps that need ASP.NET Core (Microsoft.AspNetCore.App) or WinForms/WPF (Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App) need those runtime archives unpacked into the same {runtime_dir} (they add shared/<name>/<ver>), and the plan does not include them. A patch roll-forward inside the folder works (tested: an app built for 8.0.0 ran on 8.0.31, and a netcoreapp2.1 app ran on 2.2.5 through the default Minor roll-forward). Running on a newer major needs rollForward Major/LatestMajor in the app's runtimeconfig.json (3.0+). Nothing is written outside {runtime_dir}, no registry key is created and nothing is added to PATH at install time (unlike the .exe/.msi installers, which register HKLM\SOFTWARE\dotnet\Setup\InstalledVersions and would make the copy global). At run time the diagnostics IPC uses a named pipe, not a file. Unpack only: no installer, no registry, no PATH.

prerequisites: Windows XP SP2+, Server 2003 SP1+, or Vista (the only systems where dotnetfx35.exe itself installs 3.5 SP1)

Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2: 3.5.1 is an OS component. Enable it with `dism /online /enable-feature /featurename:NetFx3 /norestart` (it is on by default on Windows 7 client) instead of running this file

Windows 8+ / Server 2012+: 3.5 is a Feature on Demand. Use `dism /online /enable-feature /featurename:NetFx3 /all /norestart`, which downloads from Windows Update, or add /source:<media>\sources\sxs /limitaccess offline. dotnetfx35.exe does not install it there
recipes.uninstall: none: leave it installed (a shared OS component; other apps may use it)
side_effects: Installs the OS-wide .NET Framework: %WINDIR%\Microsoft.NET\Framework(64)\, the GAC, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\NET Framework Setup\NDP\ registry keys, NGEN scheduled tasks and Windows Update servicing
Machine-wide and shared by every .NET Framework app; it can't be installed twice or into a chosen folder, and uninstalling it with one app would break others
May require a reboot (exit code 3010 or 1641)
recipes.min_os: Windows XP SP2 (x86/x64); on 7+ it is enabled as a Windows feature instead
recipes.notes: .NET Framework is not a private runtime. The CLR is activated through the System32 mscoree.dll shim and binds framework assemblies from the Windows GAC, so it can't be unpacked into {runtime_dir} or run from there. Extracting the package (/x) only yields MSIs that install the same machine-wide component. So the recipe is 'run the vendor installer once per machine, if missing': query the verify key first and skip when Install=1. Exit codes: 0 ok, 3010/1641 ok but reboot needed, 1603 fatal, 5100 system requirements not met. The schema has no per-Windows-version branch for steps, so the installer-builder must pick the exe (XP/2003/Vista) or the DISM command (7+) itself. Can it be avoided? Only by not using .NET Framework: an app that can be rebuilt for modern .NET should use the private runtime archives above. There is no xcopy option for Framework apps.

launch.notes: .NET Framework is part of Windows; apps start directly.

prerequisites: Windows 10 21H2+ / Windows 11 / Server 2022 (x86, x64, arm64). 4.8.1 does not install on Windows 7/8.1 (4.8 was the last for those), and XP's last is 4.0
recipes.uninstall: none: leave it installed (an in-place, machine-wide update of every 4.x)
side_effects: Installs the OS-wide .NET Framework: %WINDIR%\Microsoft.NET\Framework(64)\, the GAC, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\NET Framework Setup\NDP\ registry keys, NGEN scheduled tasks and Windows Update servicing
Machine-wide and shared by every .NET Framework app; it can't be installed twice or into a chosen folder, and uninstalling it with one app would break others
May require a reboot (exit code 3010 or 1641)
In-place update: replaces whatever 4.x was installed, so it changes the Framework used by every 4.x app on the machine
recipes.notes: Same reasoning as 3.5: .NET Framework 4.x is an OS component, activated through System32 mscoree.dll and the GAC; it can't be private or side by side (4.5-4.8.1 are in-place updates of 4.0). Detect first: Release DWORD >= 533325 means 4.8.1 is present (Microsoft: compare with >=, never ==). An app built for 4.x <= 4.8 runs on the 4.8 that ships in Windows 10 1903+ and Windows 11, so if Release >= the app's target (528040 for 4.8), skip this installer entirely. Windows 11 22H2+ already includes 4.8.1. `reg query` output is text; the installer should parse the hex value. Exit codes: 0 ok, 3010/1641 ok but reboot needed, 1603 fatal, 5100 OS not supported. Can it be avoided? Usually yes on Windows 10+ (the OS already has 4.8.x), and never on Windows 7/8.1 for an app that truly needs 4.8.1 APIs (impossible there).

launch.notes: .NET Framework is part of Windows; apps start directly.
